title: 🌲 Vaelora — Second Age Forest Courts, Hidden Towns & Reform
rawNotionMarkup: Vaelora • Second Age Years 1–1,437 in Avarran retrospective dating. The culture and chronology of Vaelora's own named eras are still open. The people here include public town dwellers, concealed communities and independent forest and lake polities. No present Crownwall city, Elderwood boundary or current dynasty is automatically founded by this history. ## The broken wards and the fear of being found (Years 1–112) Across lake settlements and deep forests, some familiar protections became unreliable as the First Age's moon-based powers were destroyed or changed. A small hidden village might find itself visible from a road for the first time in generations; a public mill town might lose the enchantment that made its bridge safe. Not all places were enchanted, and the planet's distinct World's Breath continued. the Winter of Open Doors is the local name for a wave of accidental exposures, thefts and forced migrations among a group of concealed settlements. It was not a universal catastrophe affecting every Fae court or a revelation of genuine First Age records. Some Aelwyn courts responded by offering refuge under strict, difficult-to-understand pacts. Others used the crisis to impose binding service obligations on frightened neighbors. Pixie air villages constructed physical windbreaks and narrow footbridges to avoid depending on unreliable flight magic. Brownie and Boggart families, whose precise relationship remains unknown, set up autonomous Doorstep Councils in selected towns to negotiate the terms under which small households performed labor for larger citizens. Where powerful nobles refused, families hid their craft, fled or sabotaged exploitative contracts. Their actions were political and sometimes dangerous, not charming house-servant folklore. An elderly Halfling potter, Vella Thimblefen, and an Eldar healer, Seryn Mossborne, organized the Moss-Cup Refuge, a group of visible shelters for travelers denied access to magically protected groves. A young Foxfolk courier exposed a steward who had been selling sanctuary rights. The steward was removed in one town; the practice survived elsewhere. The shelters provided ordinary beds and medicine, not compulsory magical protection. ## The arguments of roots and roads (Years 113–321) ### The Seven-Bark Compact A loose agreement among forest-edge communities, including certain Eldar grove keepers, Ent neighbors, Mushroom folk, Satyr orchards and nearby Human and Goblin settlers, negotiated the Seven-Bark Compact. Seven refers to the initial signatories, not all the peoples of Vaelora. The parties disputed timber harvest, water sources and safe paths through sacred forests. One council considered every fire destructive; another argued that controlled hearths and farmland were necessary for families to survive. Eldar judge Veraleth brokered a compromise granting fuel gathering in designated sections while prohibiting the burning of living old-growth. The agreement was broken during later shortages but established a language of shared stewardship. ### The bitter harvest of the mirror lake A small lake principality, Glassmere Court, relied on a profitable but unreliable charm to keep grain dry. When the charm failed and a severe shortage followed, its regent blamed traveling Gnome workers and imprisoned several without trial. A combined petition from Merfolk shore families, lake fishers, Gnome instrument makers and local craftspeople led to the Hearing of the Empty Barn. The court reluctantly released the prisoners, but demanded heavy restitution from them instead of acknowledging its own neglect. A later civic council paid the remaining debts from the principality's hoarded treasure. Some citizens celebrated the reform; others called it theft. Glassmere Court is an ancient local state, not an ancestor of any present capital unless later established. ## Wonder's young cities and forbidden teachers (Years 322–575) As newer lunar workings became reliable enough for sophisticated use, Vaelora developed both thriving public towns and extraordinary concealed settlements. The Lanternwater Free Quays were a federation of lake ports whose charters allowed different professions and peoples to petition government. In practice wealthy ship owners held most votes, and many workers remained excluded. A Guild of Unpaid Lights, founded by urban Pixie artisans and Human lamplighters, refused to maintain the city's enchanted signals after a wealthy magistrate tried to transfer the risk of failures to child apprentices. The strike led to pay for dangerous repair work and inspection of the physical lamps. The new arrangement did not ban apprenticeships; it limited their abuses in participating ports. ### The Fae bargain that wasn't a gift In the foothills, one independent Aelwyn court offered food and concealment to travelers during a hard season but demanded future service that some recipients had not fully understood. Neighboring human and Satyr communities argued over whether a promise made under desperation was truly binding. the Trial of the Empty Chair ended with a particular agreement that no absent or unrepresented child could be bound by a parent's bargain. The court conceded because its own younger members challenged the practice. It remained a court of bargains, mystery, generosity and danger, not a universal Fae parliament. This incident establishes no new cosmic law of magic and does not equate Aelwyn with Pixies. ## The price of shelter and beauty (Years 576–950) ### The Silk-Rain Hall A famous textile, medicine and living-architecture complex called the Silk-Rain Hall attracted artisans, scholars and merchants from varied districts. Eldar designers explored artful moon-born growth; Mushroom folk provided dye expertise; Brownie workshops made intricate practical fittings; Foxfolk factors managed shipping; a small Harpy community maintained cliff access. The complex became wealthy and was celebrated by poets, while the lower workshops were crowded and dangerous. When workers petitioned for rest days, a patron accused them of attacking art itself. the Green-Needle Boycott began when artisans refused to sell finished goods until workshop conditions were inspected. Guards arrested several organizers. Some allied merchants joined the boycott, while others quietly profited from it. The eventual Window-and-Air Charter required ventilation and access to water in qualifying work halls. A generation later, some workshops had become healthier and others forged inspection marks. The charter's mixed record is part of the history. ### The paths no one owned Some Ent assemblies opposed heavily traveled roads cutting old grove roots; some argued that restricting all roads left poor settlements at the mercy of hidden woodland lords. In one famous dispute an Ent speaker named Root-at-Dawn refused to stand aside from a proposed cutting line until the town agreed to redesign its bridge. He was patient, stubborn and capable of being wrong about the effect on poorer neighborhoods. The final route cost more, protected the grove and left a flood shelter accessible. No entire species was obligated to adopt his view, and his story is a Second Age account, not first-hand First Age documentation. ## Rich courts and people who disappear from the record (Years 951–1,321) The Coast of the White Glass contained prosperous trade cities whose beacons and markets employed Gnomes, Goblins, human sailors, Merfolk navigators and itinerant scholars. Wealthy courts funded music, healing, literary schools and new magical research. Some privately rented debt labor to prestigious academies. The Book of the Uncounted was compiled by a Brownie legal advocate, Perrin Half-Door, who recorded workers excluded from port and guild censuses. Her testimony revealed that people could sustain a beautiful city without being recognized as its full citizens. Authorities briefly banned the book; later reformers copied it, and one port extended limited civic rights to previously uncounted resident households. In woodland courts, older long-lived custodians clashed with younger Eldar students and Aelwyn participants over access to powerful new arts. Some festivals welcomed outsiders and blended carefully distinct cultural traditions; others were guarded, competitive or cruel. A charming woodland village could conceal an abusive household, and a stone trading city could contain a fiercely generous neighborhood. The difference between visible and hidden was not the difference between good and evil. ### The annual empty bowl At the end of the Avarran “Wonder” date span, the Empty-Bowl Table in a handful of lake and forest settlements fed travelers regardless of their species or ability to reciprocate. Families took turns providing a meal and telling the story of someone who had helped them when a magical convenience failed. Some local leaders resented the expense. The custom persisted in several places because farmers, cooks, laborers and children kept it alive when wealthy sponsors withdrew. Its power was ordinary hospitality rather than a new lunar miracle. ## The final 116 years and the breaking of the Age The later Lantern Orchard Councils, their medicine and forestry disputes and Orchard Reconciliation are established in the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). Those later councils need not be the same continuous institutions as the earlier Lanternwater Free Quays, Glassmere Court, or Seven-Bark Compact. The Second Age-ending earthquakes were global and destructive, but the fate of any specific Vaeloran court or capital in that catastrophe remains open. No species extinction and no Orcs in the Second Age are binding continuity. Vaelora's local names and number of eras remain to be developed.
